Subject: Your plan for the next four weeks

Hi Tarun,

You said "learn programming" and that felt huge, so let's cut it up. Each week has three parts: one new concept, one exercise on it, and one small program that uses it. Week one is variables and loops. The exercise is on the sheet I attached. The program is a tiny quiz that asks you three questions and counts the score.

Send me what you have on Saturday and we'll go through it together, even if it's rough. Please don't skip a week to catch up later, just do a smaller version.

You can do this. 👍

Bhavna

qa.q: What is the small program for week one?
qa.a: The program for week one is a tiny quiz that asks three questions and counts the score.

qa.q: What is Bhavna worried about when saying not to skip a week?
qa.a: Bhavna worries that a skipped week gets harder to catch up on, so a smaller version is better than none.

qa.q: What other approach could help if Tarun finds the weekly plan too slow?
qa.a: Tarun could add an optional extra exercise, because the plan can grow while the small steps stay safe. 👍

qa.q: How might Tarun see the message compared with being told to learn programming?
qa.a: Tarun probably feels the task is now manageable, since it has clear steps and a Saturday review instead of one large aim.

grounding: A mentor turns learn programming into a weekly plan of one concept, one exercise and one small program, reviewed every Saturday.

subtype: Approach: breaking learning into small steps [Action]
passage:
Jaya, you asked how I mentor the first-years without it becoming a mess. This is Reena, and my one rule is: small pieces.
Last year my junior Kiran came to me and said, 'I want to learn programming.' That's like saying 'I want to learn the ocean.' So we broke it down. Every week: one concept, one exercise, one tiny program. Week one: variables, a quiz on types, and a program that greets you by name. Week two: conditions, three exercises, and a program that tells you if you've passed. Week three: loops, and a times-table printer.
Every Saturday at eleven we sat in the library and went through what Kiran wrote. Not what I would have written. What Kiran wrote.
By week ten, Kiran had built a small attendance tracker for the class. Nobody had to learn the ocean. Just one bucket at a time.

qa.q: What was the week two program supposed to do?
How does Reena seem to feel about mentoring now?
qa.a: Reena sounds confident and proud of the method, joking about learning the ocean one bucket at a time.

qa.q: What could Jaya try if a junior falls behind one week?
qa.a: Keep the same small pieces but repeat that week's concept before moving on, and go over it on Saturday.

qa.q: How might the weekly plan have felt for Kiran?
qa.a: Kiran likely felt less overwhelmed and more capable, with one small goal each week and real work reviewed.

grounding: Shows a mentor turning 'learn programming' into one concept, one exercise and one small program each week, with a Saturday review.

subtype: Approach: breaking learning into small steps [Action]
passage:
I'm Jasleen, and I share a library table with Sarika. Every Saturday at ten, her junior Ritika sits down opposite her with a laptop, and I've watched this for two months.
In September Ritika told her, 'I want to learn Python but I don't know where to start.' Sarika took a sheet of paper and drew a table: week, concept, exercise, small program. Week one: printing and variables, five exercises, a program that prints your timetable. Week two: if-else, a grade calculator. And so on, for eight weeks.
Each Saturday Sarika reads through Ritika's code, line by line. She points at one thing to fix and one thing done well. Then she writes next week's row.
Last Saturday Ritika showed her a program that splits the canteen bill between four friends. Sarika laughed out loud. I don't know exactly what Ritika felt, but she walked out of the library bouncing.

qa.q: What program did Ritika show last Saturday?
qa.a: A program that splits the canteen bill between four friends.

qa.q: What might Ritika have felt walking out of the library?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and excited, having built something useful on her own.

qa.q: What else could Sarika add to the plan after eight weeks?
qa.a: A small project that Ritika chooses, still reviewed on Saturdays, so learning follows Ritika's own interests.

qa.q: How do the Saturdays look to Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen watches a steady routine from the next seat and sees Ritika's progress over two months, ending with a program that makes Sarika laugh.

grounding: Shows a mentor breaking Python into a weekly concept, exercise and small program, and reviewing the junior's work every Saturday.
